item.title: a patient review of my Sheaffer Prelude
item.description:
I don't really remember what it was that encouraged me to buy the pen I'm about to write about, nor do I really understand why it is that I feel the need to review it. It's more that I feel compelled to write about it, and that I feel compelled to run against the grain of what I think has become to norm for how it is that people review things - my intent here is not to sell you on the pen I own, nor is it to necessarily critique it. It's just that I really, really love this pen, and some part of me feels compelled to write about how much I love this pen.
I have been someone who writes by hand for as long as I can remember. In fact, it's almost a little strange that I've chosen the format in which I want to write this review, as I'm writing it on my laptop, which is steadily running out of battery, and this is usually the exact reason I love a good pen - short of running out of ink, it can't die on you, so you can always write.
Now, the reasons for writing this: I was sitting on the porch at my parent's home in Virginia, reading 'Biography of X' when I looked down at the pencil I had in my hands, a Tombow Homograph Mono, and realized that I really enjoyed the pencil for the build quality in the wood. I then remembered that I, personally, was actually influenced into buying this pencil by some random video or other to buy this pencil, and I am glad that I was. It's a good pencil!
However, the reason I think it's a good pencil is not because a reviewer told me that it was a good pencil - it's the fact that I've had a box of these pencils for about two months now, and I haven't moved on from the first one I took out of the box and sharpened. In fact, I'd have to figure that I will very likely have that (beautiful) box of pencils I purchased for $14 from the internet hate machine for several more years, because, get this - I haven't even sharpened it again.
Anyway - on to more important things: what I found myself wanting to write about is that all too often, the culture of a 'review' typical of those seen across the internet exhibits two qualities:
1. It is there to sell you something
2. Most of the time, a 'reviewer' has only been using the thing they are selling you for a couple of months.
What this means, --for me-- is that while I could write paragraphs and paragraphs about the Tombow (I already have, lamentably), I actually haven't been using it long enough for me to feel honest about how it makes me feel.
I do, however, feel that I have been using my Prelude for long enough to sing its praises, but I don't really care whether or not you get one of your own. I don't think that's the point of this particular review, rather I'm trying to influence you to go out and care about something for years and years, so much so that you are compelled to come back and tell someone else just why it is that you care about that thing so much. If nothing else, that's what I feel is missing in the 'culture' of review.
Nowadays, it's not apparent that anyone claiming to 'review' something really cares for the things they own. Or rather, maybe it's apparent that some reviewers really like what they are reviewing, but not that they like any one of the actual items that they are reviewing. It is why I find it so much more delightful when I do strike upon a video or an essay where it is apparent the reviewer really does care about the thing they are talking about, because it becomes incredibly obvious through the pronounced excitement they have for what it is that they are reviewing; it appears less that they are selling one product or another, and more that they just really, really enjoy something and want to share it with the world - which is exactly why I want to write about this pen.
The reason I love my Prelude is in part because it writes well, but there is more to it than this - so much more that I don't want to say all that much about how it writes, so I'll just do that in the following paragraph. If that's all you came to read, great, we're already succeeding, and you won't need to go any further. If not, there are (I just counted) 25 more paragraphs beyond the following that explain why it is that how the pen writes is not the point:
The Sheaffer Prelude I bought in 2020 writes very well. It is perfectly balanced when posted, and it has a wonderful brassy patina from years upon years of use. It has a black nib. The pen clip broke off in 2024 (I think). I have tried many other pens since getting it, and the only reason I have tried this other pens is because I am now deathly afraid that one day I will lose or break the pen I have been faithfully using as my main driver for the last 7 years, and the emotional vaccuum it leaves behind will be incredibly difficult to fill.
This brings me to what I actually want to write about: I have a deep, appreciative, and loving relationship with this pen, not due to the fact that it is a good pen, but because I have written so much with it, and it has been through so much with me. My opinion has become that this is why my particular Sheaffer Predule is special. It is not just that the pen has survived what I estimate to have been 1.7 million words of writing (that's around 30 192-page notebooks at around ~300 words per page), but that because of this, it is a higher quality pen than the pen I started with, and not just because it's 'broken in'.
I read Pirsig's 'Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance' in the middle of my junior year of college, where he supposes that beyond the definition of most words, making the effort to define 'quality' is an increasingly impossible task. Unfortunately, I am one who is given to impossible tasks; that year I handed in a hand-written essay in response to an Anthropology Midterm that wasn't directly responding to the prompt offered in which I wrote out exactly what I suppose to be my definition of quality: quality is the history behind an object.
The basic treatise following my definition was this: a high quality object is something that has, in some form or other, embodied the story of how it came to be that object. I want to eschew the clinical definition of quality meaning craftsmanship because I do think the two are distinct. I think it is possible for a person to own something cheap and badly made and for it to have higher quality than something comparable that is more expensive and better made provided the relationship between the person who owns the object is more pronounced than that of higher percieved craftsmanship. It's for this reason that I think we find it difficult to detach ourselves from things that we have had for a long time and that have served us well - these things have taken more quality than they had when we first procured them. There is a floor to this, of course, in which a possessed object can be of such cheap materials and craft that being presented with an object with any level of substantially better mixture of the material and craft immediately outweighs the relationship of an owner and the object, but only if the owner feels that way. If not, the cheaper thing is harder to give up, and is as a result subjectively higher quality, and (as Pirsig would agree, I think) quality can only be subjective.
I could give you an example here, but I'm sure it was really hard for you to buy a better coffeetable than the one you lugged around from apartment to apartment for ten years until the exact moment where you realized what a piece of shit it was relative to something that dramatically outweighed your relationship with it and poof, the coffeetable's relationship with you is broken. As a counter, someone comes to your house and says 'your coffee table is a piece of shit' before you have the money to get one, but you immediately reflect on the fact that you lugged it around for 10 years, rolled joints on it, hit your shin on it while falling off in the course of making out with the first love of your life, and that would make it higher quality. We develop relationships with things, and I think it is the constellation of relationships of subjects with objects that give objects their quality.
What this means is that the reason an object of higher craftsmanship than the shitty coffee table (such as a substantially better coffee table) is so obviously the case is because we immediately think of the prior relationships the object has to the subjects that created it; a shitty coffee table from Ikea was produced at a factory by a machine, a higher-quality, woodworker-made coffee table was made be a person, and we intuitively can understand the relationship between that object, the person who made it, and the fact that it has been passed on to us as a record of their work, causing us to have a relationship with the object that might lead us toward caring for the object a lot more.
Now that I have sufficiently exhausted rewriting the gist of the exact essay I think I wrote for that mid-term (I did not intend to, but I did, I am sorry), maybe you can understand why this pen matters to me.
In the years since I established this definition for myself, I promptly forgot it. The reason is that I was broke, and I could not afford to care about things, other than those things I could barely afford and to which I built a relationship. Whether or not this is the 'correct' definition of and treatise for quality has never mattered too much to me as the fact that I took (and I think all of us have taken) it to be the case. I have owned lots of 'things' since I read that essay, and when I had the money to buy things that would last longer, I started buying them, strictly because they would last longer.
In particular, the pen I wrote that essay with for that particular Anthropology mid-term was a black plastic fountain pen that I stole from the University of Georgia Student Bookstore repeatedly because I wanted to write with a fountain pen. The reason I wanted to write with a fountain pen was not because I was, yes, the person who walked around campus barefoot with an Egyptian merchant's hat on my head and a leatherbound notebook in my hands1, but because I did actually grow up somewhere that taught me how to write with a fountain pen. The reason I stole the pen (repeatedly) was because a) I kept breaking them because they were really shitty pens and b) fuck the University of Georgia Student Bookstore. I would open the packaging, remove the pen, and leave, no one the wiser, free to use the pen until the nib eventually folded on itself and stopped writing, leading me, again, to go steal another one from the store. I think I did this four time over my tenure.
After I left school, I think I was able to keep using that particular 'Pen and Ink' (yes, that was the name of the brand) fountain pen before the complete crap aluminium nib shifted and ink stopped flowing. For years thereafter, I began a search for the ideal cheap pen, cycling through the Zebras and Uniballs (I am sorry, I absolutely HATED the Uniball Vision Needle that everyone wanted me to use) until I landed on the Uniball Roller Eco, which I wrote with for several years. The reason? It was unassuming, wrote (fairly) well, was cheap, and the pen clip was narrow and thin enough that I could usually assault the spine of my moleskines, then shinolas with the obligation to let me slot it in.
Unfortunately, one particular niggling aspect of the Uniball Roller Eco is that it is a piece of shit, weighing nothing, and requires remarkably substantial continuous pressure over long writing period from one's hand in order to remain consistent. The other niggling aspect of the Uniball Eco that is true of a lot of cheap things: when you buy lots of a cheap thing so that you don't care that much when you lose it, you eventually hit a wall where you are so annoyed with the fact that you have purchased so much of that cheap thing instead of buying one of a nice thing for the same price of all of those boxes that you decide, you know what, I'm going to just go ahead and buy the nice thing, and because it's a nice thing, I'll have to care where it is instead of continuously turning to look for a pen when you wanted to write something down only to discover that it has magically disappeared, shrugging your shoulders, and moving on.
And so, it was 2020. I rode my bicycle from Brooklyn to The Fountain Pen Hospital on Warren Street in lower Mannhattan, having decided on the pen using the Sheaffer website after two weeks of research and having called them to check if they had it in stock. I knew nothing about fountain pens other than the fact that I liked writing with them, that my last fountain pen was sort of horrible, cheap, and overpriced (again, a very hearty FUCK you, UGA Student Bookstore). The woman who sold the pen to me had the most Long Island accent a reader can dream up, didn't seem to comprehend the momentousness of the event at hand, selling it to me and turning around to walk back over to the Montblancs.
Now, of course, there is a breaking-in period with fountain pens. I didn't know that, so I thought, a week into writing with it and it started to 'railroad', that I'd gotten a lemon. Railroading3 is when part of the line you are writing ends up with a void in the middle, but the ink still flows around this void, leaving parallel tracks. Disaster.
Unfortunately, this happened at a time where I had left New York on assignment, so I couldn't go back to the store during the return period and beg them to give me a new one. The other option I had was to come back from that assignment and ask Sheaffer to warranty the pen, since this is something that was offered by the manufacture - but I was afraid they might not let me do that so soon after getting it, or that they might only give me one warranty replacement, and I didn't want to burn that so soon after getting it.
What that meant is that somewhere in the middle of that assignment, I had no option but to keep writing. This is where I learned the great, magical thing about fountain pens: the problem did fix itself, and the railroading behavior decreased with time. There is a less-than-magical (but still wonderful) reason for this, which (as I mentioned) is that fountain pens break in with use: they are often tipped with a pliable metal that wears as you write with them until it matches your particular writing style. It's not the case that I realized this, necessarily, because what I thought instead was 'fuck you pen, I paid for you, so you are what I'm writing with now', and as the behavior slowly vanished my awareness, I began not to think about the pen at all when I wrote, and only when I wasn't. The pen became an extension of my hand, and I wrote with tremendous ease, and I forgot that the pen was there.
The other thing that happened was that I developed an anxiety about the pen that was exactly what I'd been missing with all of the cheap Uniball Roller Ecos; I was now consistently aware of where my notebook was were specifically because my pen was in it, and the two of them together were of high value2 to me. I couldn't afford to buy another pen, and I didn't want to.
Unfortunately, two months into owning the pen and having broken it in, one day the cap liner became removed from the body of the cap, and the black nib of the pen would no longer stay inside of the cap when I pressed them together. I was devastated, and I emailed Sheaffer directly, asking them to warranty the pen. It turned out the email didn't work, so I called them and they very kindly shipped out a warranty replacement for me, asking me to send in the old pen in the same box of shipment. When the new pen arrived, the nib in the box was silver, rather than the black that I'd been writing with, and I'd just gone through that painful breaking-in period and I liked the black nib better, so I put the old cap on the new pen, then shipped off the two together.4 An interesting side-effect of this that I only found out while writing this essay is that the pen that they shipped me was actually not the same pen model. The black nib is what identified my pen as the 'PVD' model of the Prelude, and they had shipped me the 'Standard' model. What this means is that the cap I have on my pen is NOT the fancy PVD cap (boo) but the rest of the pen is.
This new hybrid pen and I continued a long, close relationship wherein notebook upon notebook were filled, chronicling a change of career, new responsibilities, new relationships, and so on. At some point, the pen clip removed itself from the body after having been stressed to its mechanical limit from being jammed into too many moleskine spines, and I coped with the sharp fangs left behind that wore down into the nubs the pen has today.
I don't know exactly when it was, but at some point in the fortuitous journey of increasing my net worth through a change of career, I realized that I could probably buy another, better pen, or at the very least a companion to this pen, and so I began trying out others. The interesting thing is that I have hated literally every other pen I have purchased because my Prelude is broken in and I love writing with it. However, this fact terrifies me, because I have now written so much with this pen that the prospect of having to find a replacement feels more like an obligation than it does something I am actually interested in doing. I find myself frequently thinking that I need to 'retire' the pen, constantly steeled against a certainty that lives in the back of my mind like crouched gargoyle staring at me from the shadows, telling me that one day, I will lose the pen and never get it back.
I should be clear I have actually lost this pen before. I have the vague recollection of having lost it with my passport and my notebook to the back of an airplane seat sometime just after the pandemic made flying okay again, and it was the only time a notebook I lost ever made its way back to me. I left it on the table at Little Grenjai in 2025 and the Kiwi woman who worked behind the counter set it aside to make sure it got back into my hands. Most recently, I was on a date with my current partner, who I wasn't yet dating at the time, and both watched the pen roll off the edge of a table at a restaurant. My being a gangly fool whose response to things falling is not to immediately reach for them because that is likely to exacerbate the falling by launching the falling thing further into obscurity, instead having programmed myself to watch and listen for where something falls - we watched it roll toward the drain, causing my now partner to leap from her seat and grab it before it fell through the stormdrain. This is one of many reasons I am with this woman today.
The body of the pen is 'brassed' to hell. In fountain pen circles, this denotes a 'well-loved' pen. It is so; I love this pen more than I probably should, a dangerous, unrelenting love that hopes feverishly never to culminate in loss. A love that is the reason I plugged in my laptop 5 hours ago and kept writing.
It's possible that this is how 'reviewers' are made - one acquires an understanding of what a good 'thing' is and as a result go about trying to compare everything to it so that they can relive the experience of having loved something. It's probably the same reason that people immediately 'get another dog' when their dog passes, because it's a desire to fill a hole that opens up when you build a relationship with something that isn't you. The quality of the things in our lives increase as we build relationships with them. Quality is what allows us to appreciate the space that something takes up in our lives and the relationship we have to it, whether it is because we understand the life that made the object, or because we lived with it. It is what compels us to care about things, or for them, whether they are sentient or not. I look at my pen as the time that I have spent writing, maybe more than I do the words themselves, and it shows. We don't get many things in life to care about at that level, because we caring creatures don't live that long.
The point is this: don't go out there looking at reviews expecting that anyone will do what I am trying to do here, because it's probably not the same thing. I think most reviews or testimonials are an attempt to serve as a starting point for the relationship you are going to have with whatever you're researching. What I am telling you is that the quality of what you are allowing to enter your life is shaped by how you build a relationship with it, and I am begging you to do so.
I'll close with this: there is a video of a woman ridiculing her husband because he had reached the end of a spool of wire he had purchased in high school. She doesn't understand the relationship between he and the spool of wire, but he does. I don't care for the social commentary that surrounds this on the internet about their relationship, because it is a question of answering and understanding one thing: the quality of the wire did not matter when he bought it. the quality mattered when he reached the end of that spool, and was faced its loss, a tiny perforation threading the wire through each object into which he had placed it, far into the past, to the moment he began his relationship with the object.

  2. yes hello Pirsig ↩

  3. (get your mind out of the gutter, this is an essay about pens, not penises) ↩

A few notes here: a) You used to be able to talk to people on the phone at the companies that made the things you owned, and I miss this time in our history, because it meant you had a human connection with the things you owned. b) It turns out that at the time Sheaffer offered a Limited Lifetime Warranty for an unlimited number of replacements... which are now only a warranty of two or three years after purchase after William Penn bought the brand from A.T. Cross in 2022 and negated all prior responsibilities Shaeffer has to honor the previous company's warranties. There go my chances of an affiliate link. d) The white dot on the top of the Sheaffer finneal (the top of the pen) used to be the symbol that signified the company's unerring Limited Lifetime Warranty. Now it just means 'it's a Sheaffer' and we used to do that. ↩

item.title: I hate Sam Kriss and I don't even know him, but at least he's human
item.description:
You know what would be cool? If a person could hold a device up to their face and speak with abandon, moving through the mildly connective fabric of their thoughts in order to tease out a meaning, then tell their device to arrange those thoughts spoken into an essay that others might read, taking out all the difficult intermediate steps of what makes writing an essay so hard, then post it to social media and manage all the posting that is also so hard, and then, finally, all the critique that comes with having released a thought into the world - which is also so, so hard. That would be great, wouldn't it? To have optimized all the thinking out?
A couple of days ago, as though the poles reversed, I found myself thinking that I no longer want to use AI to check my work or any of my writing, ... or any of my thoughts, either - because I think I finally understand the itching sensation at the back of my neck that feels wholly unsatisfied by AI's claim to be a digital mirror. I'd been using Claude for that purpose, and now I get why I can't - it can't give me what it is that I'm actually looking for, because what I'm really looking for is validation.
The reason was in part the fact that while reading an article by Sam Kriss, I realized that he was going to kill me for doing what I've been doing. I immediately threw up my hands - I don't want to die!I don't really use Claude to write, necessarily. I use it to convert my handwritten writing into text (it's remarkably good at that) and I use it to... shamefully, make myself feel better about my writing. I use AI for validation that what I'm saying is something that anyone might read.
I'm realizing that writing and reasoning is exactly the wrong place for a tool that strings together ideas without really understanding what a writer is trying to get at, or without actually paying attention to whether or not there's a connection in the first place (fun fact, there's a name for that). I'm done doing that, because it doesn't lead me anywhere. Despite those who created AI hoping that it can do so. the sort of reasoning AI is capable of is the sort of reasoning required for mechanism - an answer to a question that is generated by a pattern. That is where it serves the purpose, and I think it's very good at that - good enough that
What this means, to me, is that Sam Kriss probably won't come to my house to kill me, or at the very least won't stand in my living room shouting a tirade of well-phrased cwitticisms (I'm reaching) about how it is that writing is holy and important and deserving of protection. I already get it, and he's right to post a reactionary screed designed to cause outrage. We are outraged. That's the point. Part of this is that I can tell, from reading his words, that he's a human, because he holds positions that I disagree with, and in fact that I hated.
I hated the fragmented reasoning in the middle of Kriss' screed when he says of writer Hanania that "whenever I see anything from Richard Hanania I’m seized by an overwhelming desire to demolish his house", "because I'm Jewish and he's Palestinian". I hated it because it felt human, because I could imagine a person at the other end of the digital tangle sitting in front of their computer and dreaming up the most rage-inducing sentence he could come up with, and because it's the whole reason the essay works.
It is, of course, the exact section that has been clipped and reposted in the day or so since he posted what he did, exactly because it's a horrid thought, and because the circular reasoning that makes it simultaneously anti-semitic and racist against Palestinians is exactly the sort of wordsmithy that causes anyone to stop and contemplate a little longer reasoning period Claude cheerfully puts below a query. I'm still thinking about it, and I read it yesterday, turning it over and over in my head because it was designed to make me angry and because everything else Kriss says in the essay is compelling enough to go back and read again; I excitedly want to express that I do, in fact, appreciate that a horrid opinion about how to treat a group of people is something that makes his writing feel human.
The humanistic impulse in me to say that the two things are not connected--that belonging to a faith shouldn't mean that he wants to commit xenocide--, are the nuclear missile that Kriss is sending to my house from across the internet. It might have been a self-deprecating joke, but it was a bad one designed to be bad, and that's great, and that's my point. Slow clap, it worked. The rest of the essay is fantastic, for the same human, angry reason that jumps out of the text and that I, for one, am still dwelling on. I've already seen any number of rage-fueled takes to the fact that he wrote those words for us to consume, but hey, at least it was human.
This is not an essay against AI, necessarily. I don't want to it to be (I don't even know if it's an essay), but it might end up that way. It seems stupid and ill-conceived that I feel compelled to bring it in to the discussion, because maybe there really is a compulsion within all of us to comment eternally on the present moment.
I know that those among us who care about the sanctity of the word should never hazard to touch the stove on which the kettle is whistling just to see if it's hot - not because I think it's normal to touch the stove, because we're purists and idealists and all the other lists that we use to make ourselves up, but I'm also a realist. I know that sometimes the intrusive appel du vide shows up unbidden and asks us if maybe we should try touching the stove because there may be a quantum chance that just this once it won't be too hot to touch. It's the reason that I do use AI for other purposes - I can tell there's a place for it, and I do use it that way - it feels like a superpower to use it in ways I am undereducated to do otherwise.
However, I am realizing that AI's utility does not belong among my words, my thoughts or anything that urges me toward presentiment and experience and tries to tease out meaning. It's not me doing performing the action and hating the process, it's a machine that I want to do the hard part for me. I am not an AI apologist, because I don't give a shit what you think about me, so I'm not going to describe myself that way. These are just words I'm using to navigate a thought. That's what writing is, after all.

See, readers and writers fall in love with sentences. It's not the paragraph or even the arc of the novel, the essay, whatever, that attracts us. It's the reason that one sentence stood out to me from the many other very good ones Kriss wrote in an essay that had nothing to do with the core subject matter. Most good thoughts are an attempt to reach across the blackness of space between ideas and draw out inference from their connection, and then the hope is that by having drawn that connection, we can derive meaning from the pattern we see connecting them. A good sentence is a window into how a writer sees the world - but there's a thing about windows; if we know that people are going to be looking in, we arrange the room with this knowledge in mind. We use our taste (hah!) to decide what we want people to see in that room and how we want it to be received by them. A good sentence is and act of synthesis, compressing a body of knowledge into a pane of glass.
Every stereotype of a tech bro is a mattress on the floor because no one will ever see the inside of their mind and the machine we are building is more important than our wellbeing. That's the reason the room we're looking at doesn't look like anything, why the takeout boxes haven't been thrown out, and what justifies the impulse to throw this entire fucking essay in the trash before publishing it.
We cannot expect words to do this on their own, even if we draw a semantic map of the likelihood that one word will be connected to another, and then use that map to automate the performance of connection. Part of the promise of AI is that it can do this - that the semantic map will somehow generate the patterns we seek. In some circumstances, it works -- but when we're trying to come up with something that matters to us and outsourcing the reasoning to a pattern generator, it's really just graphomania. It doesn't mean anything specific, because it was written by no one, for no one, from no one's perspective, with the mixed expectation that an unknowing public will read it.
Graphomania as a condition was described long before Milan Kundera asserted that it is a symptom of a society too docile and comfortable to do anything other than write and believe that their writing is worth reading. I've been realizing that people have fallen out of knowing the term - but there's even a clinical definition that comes from having one's temporal lobe affected - an affliction that causes words to spill forth from someone's hand and onto the page without actually reaching a point.
I have a long history with that particular fragment of The Book of Laughter and Forgetting - it was what caused me spend the last fifteen years thinking I couldn't write because my impulse to write was really just a manic impulse. I spent fifteen years mulling over the impact of those few sentences in order to conclude that I fucking hate Kundera for communicating an egotism that delineates the difference between writing with an impulse to explain something and writing because one has an impulse to write. While I am glad that happened, it's also incredibly frustrating to think that we should somehow stop short of expressing ourselves. There's a balance to be struck, after a

When I think about Vivian Maier's photography, it gives me a similar sensation to that when I think of graphomania - a compulsion to have created something, but uncertain of why. Maybe it was just a hobby that she got good at, maybe even something that had to do with teh dynamics of privilege while living in a society that did not deem women legitimate in teh creation of their art (indeed, she and Virginia Woolf were contemporaries, which I don't think is brought up often enough)
I think of the urge to document, ot keep everything that comes with wanting to live in a society that has given us the means to doso. I think it's atrocious, in some sense, biut I also think it's rpbobably the case that living in the midst of society causes us to think that society is pretty gtreaty a nd that because of that it's somethign that needs to be preserved - so maybe there is, in some sense, value to the action.

item.title: Dust Becoming Conscious
item.description:
I think life is a consequence
I think life is a consequence of having tried to become more than the dust we were born to be, that we are consciousness that emerged from the universe considering too deeply whether or not there is purpose
I think life is a consequence and because of it we are tasked with the frustration of living, of coming up against the knowledge that only we can create meaning, and that when these atoms of dust came together to become who we are, we were already destined to fail
I think life is a consequence but I think this consequence is beautiful, and because of the dust we're made from we're required to consider the irrelevance of our existence, that these atoms of dust that gathered in the storm of possibility are something more than just dust, they are beautiful and we are beautiful
but I think that this consequence is a cost incurred, it's something that we'll always carry as a burden, always forced into the act of living as though a rebellion against the entropy of time, and I think that consequence is something we'll carry until our dying breath

item.title: Why Reading Matters
item.description:
I have to remember what I have learned and why it is important to read theory and fiction.

"You should read more" comes from a place of deep misunderstanding about the generalized unrest people it is not a question of a life lived in the context of new ideas, but rather the people can or should be learning constantly. It's my loose contention that learning constantly provides us with the tools to deal with the problems with me encounter, but I am deeply cognizant of the teleological gap that arises in not having one's own needs, met at a basic level and the encouragement to educate oneself. After all, we cannot fill stomachs with words.

This is maybe the place from which to make the most significant inquiry of what uses education if the utility of this education cannot be implemented due to systemic barriers placed in the path of resilience the pen is only mightier than the sword given the paper on which to communicate ideas without the means to transmit into action, the philosophy, we hope to inspire people with violence seems well positioned to take the shape of action little inspired by anything other than a desire to cease or ease one's suffering.

It is often addressed in films this way how do the well-intentioned deviate from the morality when pinned like a fly to the Styrofoam backboard of a world so feebly built to support us? Morality is in this case situation--we can only build better worlds if we have the means to.

But we do continue to fight. We remember that those who have fought longest and hardest are those who continue to do so when every other person ceases to this is because it is the case that people who have never felt safe, will forever stay the course of seeking such safety.--and it is my contention that apathy(including my own) likely comes from a place of significant privilege.

That is--I know I will be fine and this is the reason I have the security to feel ease: I can only do so because I can consider the absurdity of having to make choices to keep myself alive, further under emphasizing that I experienced an increased degree of general attendance in the circumstance of any threat to my well-being. I will in almost every frame of reference (save one glaring circumstance, obvious to those who know me well) be fine, probably. This is the reason I can sit back on my heels and feel frustrated not with whether or not I have the means to survive, but instead how I specifically would like to survive.

Meaningfully it very much, could be the case that the reason I possessed the self-awareness to acknowledge this truth is due to the singular and unique circumstance of my own personal oppression--maybe I would otherwise be completely ignorant to my security if I didn't have to face one particular imposing fear upon my existence that call into question the security otherwise experience. I don't know because I only know my own experience to start with.

However, this last observation is important and serves to represent the final tail-eating point of what I write here. I can only speak to my own experience and it's commonality with that of others.--but I could not conceive of the relatability of my experience to parallels or lack there of without seeking out that same parallelism. It is critically this seeking out that impart to the act of reading and learning about both the real and fictional experiences of others it's critically importance. I may not be conscious of it, but every time I imagine the existence of the "other", I glean some small understanding of the parallax between our identities, and my hope is that with each of the perambulations into the possibility space existing between experiences, I am opening up just a bit more to the possibility within me to engage in a sympathetic residence with them I do not know if this is true, but it is what I like to believe. A combination of qualitative appreciation between the differences of shared realities, and most importantly, the sheer obligation to utilize my imaginative skill, requires me an obligation to as well grow as a person.

This, if among less weight and morally oriented, justifications, is why I read. I read to better understand myself, and to understand other others, and it works, more often than not. Better yet, I think (I think) it gives me hope.

I'll close by invoking someone else's words from a book I needed to read when I did:

Rebecca Solnit -

item.title: On healing and slowness
item.description:
I think I've been going through a period of healing. The general sense I gather is that some of this is coming from a desire to incorporate more slowness into my life, a sense of living that allows me to stop and pay attention to my current surroundings, rather than those I am examining at some undetermined period of time in a distant future. Some of this has come in the form of a moralism with respect to how it is that we engage with one another as human beings; in a networked era, we believe we must communicate with everyone who can listen to us and that every opinion is equally important, but I'm not really convinced that this is a good way of being, because it requires us to think of everyone who we can interact with as a form of audience rather than a community.
Some of the healing that I've been engaging with is a particular kind of slowness that corresponds to trying to acknowledge who it is in my life that I actually care about and with whom I want to deepen my relationships. It turns out that the number of social media followers that you have nor the number of attempts that you've made to increase that number actually give you any moral or emotional well-being. As Ed Yong put it, you should cultivate an audience, not followers.
I suppose some of this writing is an attempt to return to those who have taken on the honor of signing up for this newsletter - So far it's been something that I only release one every sometimes, but I assure you that every time I write it, I do think about the importance of having written it and the importance of why I am sharing thoughts with the people who are receiving it in the first place. This is maybe where the moralism comes into play; a sort of pseudo-social attempt to get people to listen to what I have to say as though what I'm saying has any worth and it really doesn't. Backing off of that sort of self-deprecation is a parallel thought that keeps me considering that in fact I'm not trying to convince any one of you of anything at all but rather simply trying to communicate.
I think the present era does a really good job of making us believe that all of the things we say must be somehow important or relevant or a sort of commentary on the present era, and putting ourselves in the boundary of having to express ourselves in this way, I think is mostly just exhausting and takes away from our ability to interact with one another as equal human beings.
There is a section of Milan Kundera's Book of Laughter and Forgetting where he comments on a writer speaking with a fan who walks up to him in a diner and asks for advice about how she can get into writing. He asks her why it is that she thinks she should be writing. She responds that it's possible that some people might want to read what she has to say. The author sitting at the diner bench turns to her and says, "why would you think that you had anything important to say?" I think back on this quote often whenever I start to write, because it is a form of self-deprecation - Imposter syndrome for a writer made material as though to point out that there really is no point in writing in the first place and that you should really just pack it up and go home and not even try.
I don't really think this is what Kundera was attempting to convince people of and in the years since I first read that section of his novel, I've instead found myself thinking that maybe what he's saying is that you should ask yourself critically why it is that what you are writing about is something that you want people to read. I still don't really have an answer, but I think I've stopped getting in my own way in the search for one, instead allowing the words to flow and sort of drift into purposelessness as a form of expression that attempts to connect with other people. None of us really have anything important to say. That's not the point. While maybe the author in his novel is intended as a jaded old careerist who cannot understand why he himself has written up to that point. Even his writing can be unimportant, No matter his readership. So is mine. So is yours.
This contrasts with the sentiment I've been holding around the idea that social media is something valuable in terms of how it is that we articulate our thoughts to an audience. The difference between Ed Yong's description of what fans/followers are against an audience is the difference between trying to cultivate a mob of people who you want to listen to everything you have to say versus a group of people to whom you have something very specific to say. The latter version offers people agency and the former is really just a thinly veiled attempt to self-aggrandize.
The social media profiles that fascinate me the most are those with the incredible voices who have turned off comments on any of their posts - they take distance from the work that they are creating in such a way as to understand that those who choose to read what they are working on are not necessarily people they are trying to convert, but rather people with whom they are trying to converse. Another one of Ed Yong's comments comes to mind here. "Don't argue with strangers on the internet".
Other fragments of the reading that I've been doing lately have been from authors who are reconciling a shared narrative about accelerated, networked growth as a function of technological advancement, and then those who are attempting to remember what it means to be human in absentia of this supposed progress has brought us. This latter half are those who have left behind the purported advantages of an interconnected parasocial pseudo-presence and have instead found kindness in the smallness of the world they decide to surround themselves with - people who fell into deep burnout as a function of continuing to follow the ever accelerating machine, only to be spit out and to acknowledge that we as individuals have our own needs that exist outside of the system that attempts to use us for its own purposes.
As a result of this, I think some of the healing that I am taking on or attempting to steer myself toward is reacting to a desire not to put myself into the burnout I have witnessing people (mostly men) continue to obsess over. I have over and over incorporated the "grindset" attitude to my own work and come out with next to nothing, only to realize that what was most fruitful is to focus on the most important things with the highest amount of effort in the shortest possible amount of time in order to achieve it. This sort of effort is far more rewarding because oftentimes getting into the flow of this sort of work only requires knowing exactly how you want to approach it and then putting forth the effort to ensure that you actually do. I found that this is the sort of work that comes from the product of writing out what it is that I intend to do rather than simply reacting to what I think feels like the next most important thing.
This brings me to the lesson that I feel I've been learning more recently through this period of healing and that I hope others are starting to witness in themselves because I am one to believe that we are all conduits of the society that surrounds us: we already have everything we need.
No amount of algorithmically-directed consumption is going to teach us self-worth, nor will it be what informs us of what we within ourselves deem important. If media is used as the tool, it is possible for us to reflect on what we consume against what we know ourselves, but it is more likely to put us in service of further consumption - the conscientiousness required for us to ensure that we are the vehicles of our own intention is often outweighed by the intentions of the system that feed us the knowledge we believe is informing this perspective. 'Importance' is something we have to investigate within ourselves - a thing we inquire and unpack by virtue of focused, concentrated, attentive, and most importantly loving work. It does not require this work to be continuous, but rather simply focused and attentive.

I write this out of a desire to remind myself that much of my writing is about this question of importance, but that this importance does not require others to believe that what I deem as important need be what they themselves also see as such. It also means that writing anything at all and sharing it with the small constellation of people who have chosen to read what I write doesn't require me to hold what I have to say to such a high standard as to believe that what I am saying is necessarily important rather than just a conversation.

Writing these posts, however intermittent, is an attempt to connect in a way that doesn't feel so costly through a medium that feels more conciliatory and meaningful to me in particular. If I bring you along on the journey, then that's fine, and that's fantastic, and I'm glad this conversation can be something that we are all a part of - but it doesn't oblige me to consider what it is that I am saying as somehow important in the broader sense. I don't get to decide that for any of you. I can only decide the importance relative to my own scales.

So the healing I'm taking on is to remember that what I think is important is beautiful just because I think it's important, and that I don't need to necessarily find a group of people who also believe the same thing I do because I think that's mostly what's destroyed our ability to relate to one another. If you read this and you connect to it somehow, that's wonderful. And maybe that was the point of writing, but not necessarily out of a desire to change your mind.

Maybe this writing is a form of thanks for choosing to have received this in the first place, whether or not you believed that this writing would reach you. It's to say I'm glad that you think I have something worth saying. It's to say I am glad that you are participating in my healing with me. It's to say that just possibly we have been doing things in a way that destroys our ability to find common experience and instead has put us in a position of requiring ourselves to be enraged by the continuous onslaught of information that is at once irrelevant and unimportant to our ability to live balanced quotidian lives. It's not to say that some of the more important things won't somehow reach out and affect your life directly, and I know this. But finally it is to say that yes, I do believe I am glad that you are an audience to me.

-

item.title: A Canticle for the Mind's Eye
item.description:
Falling. It's hard to say if it is a dream because the falling is taking so long that the falling has become normal, and in the deep darkness of my descent it could have be mistaken for flying, I think.

My hands in the air play small resistance with passing but maybe that is a breeze. Maybe I'm not falling or flying. Maybe I am floating. Maybe I am not alive at all.

A pinprick is all I can see and it is why I suppose that I am falling, I turn this way and that way and that little point stay below me. I think it is below me. I think gravity is pulling me toward it. I don't know if gravity is actually pulling me toward it. I can't remember how I leaned what gravity is. So maybe it's not gravity. I don't know. But there is a pinprick of light and I can't remember how I learned about gravity.

I am not sure if I am afraid because I also can't remember ever being afraid before, or rather I'm realizing I don't think I remember anything at all and I think this scares me too but I also can't remember if this feeling is anything new, but my heart is in my chest (I think) and it is bump bump bumping faster than it was a moment ago before I was trying to figure out if I was afraid and my eyes are dry from the wind or the breeze and I'm cold on one side of my body from the wetness that just sprang across my skin. I don't know if I am falling and I don't know if I am afraid and I don't like not knowing anything and I don't know where I am.

I try to think about anything and there is a jumble of concepts like "mathematics" and "Hustvedt's unification constant" but I don't really remember who Hustvedt is or why I know about her how I know she is a woman or really what a woman is because I'm just falling and experiencing something I'm not sure I have felt before and that pinprick is the only thing I can see. I think it might be brighter. Good, at least my frame of reference is changing but what is a "frame of reference" and why am I hearing myself think so loudly when I can't hear anything else, so I shout and I can hear my voice more like a bark into nothing and I realize that my throat is so dry and I'm so thirsty, my eyes hurt too and I close them and the pinprick winks out.

Good. So I can close my eyes. I should again and it doesn't carry, it sounds like shouting into cotton but I can't remember how I know what cotton is. But I can close my eyes and the pinprick goes away, so maybe I can gather the noisy haze of my thoughts into something logical or at the least something I can steer like maybe Hustvedt's unification constant is something worth knowing and maybe cotton is important.

It's difficult in the noise of my heart beating faster and these concepts racing through me to make sense of what is more important than anything else. I know what a pinprick is and I know what a pin is and I know that Hustvedt's unification constant is the numerical limit at which the barrier to consciousness interacts with a quint momentarily cooled to 0 degrees Kelvin, where consciousness is denoted by the bitflip of states within which incoming information can be processed by an extant system across the boundaries of connected interstitial state engines all reacting to the same manifold of inputs at a predictive rate constituting processor-type memory within the system. A system is a set of interacting state engines within which the flow of motivating forces inform local transformations between states for each component interacting in relation to another, and when I open my eyes I can see that the pinprick is definitely a little bit brighter but when I close my eyes I can't see it, so maybe when I close my eyes it's just not real, as though locally there's some transformation of reality that collapses into existence when I open my eyes.

I keep my eyes closed for a while, which eventually feels a bit better because I am not wondering about the pinprick and I'm done thinking about why I know what Hustvedt's constant is, so I tell myself I'll just keep them closed for a while longer. It's a bit nicer in the darkness honestly and thinking about whether or not I could see the pinprick has meant I'm not dealing with all the racing thoughts that were trying to make sense of themselves but I'm still pretty thirsty and that's making my heart beat a little faster but maybe I can just not think about that. Can I remember anything other than concepts? It doesn't really seem that's the case but I'm counting out the numbers of Pi pretty far and I seem to know a fair number of primes and that's calming so I'm just counting those in my head as well since I seem to know a lot of them.

I've been here a long time, I realize. I don't know how long I've been here but I am starting to wonder if maybe I've just been falling for so long that I don't really remember when I was first falling and if I've already thought all of this any number of times, it's just been so long since I last thought all of it that I can't remember. This, again, scares me but that can't possibly true because I can't possibly have been thirsty for this long and it's a small gnaw at my stomach that makes me think I maybe haven't been falling for that long because someone who has been falling for a long time would probably me a lot hungrier and a lot thirstier, and I open my eyes to ponder this and oh god the pinprick is brighter but I can see what it is a little better now and it looks like a little more than just a pinprick, it has a shape.

But there's nothing else here for me to look at so I'm getting curious about it and allowing myself to feel the fear of looking at it and trying to figure out what's coming, and I realize that maybe it's something I can just barely make out, it's a shape I can recognize but oh god its an eye, just barely big enough for me to see it. I realize maybe I'm moving toward it and it's actually maybe even getting bigger as I look at it, but it's just this giant unblinking eye staring back at me in the middle of all this blackness where I can't even tell what direction I'm falling in.

item.title: On a religion made of rubber and salt
item.description:
After several years of covering running, I began running in 2019.

In the years leading to the present that love has fallen apart and come back together several times, as many religions do. My faith in movement has been shaken, dusted off, and rooted more firmly by the miles that sew it together.

These have been the years where running has migrated from intrigue, to mental health tool, to injury, to fatigue, to an imperative and finally into a form of freedom. This transition had to do with the pandemic and with changing states of self, but it also had to do with realizing there was something more in the staccato of other people's footfalls that I'd been chasing beyond merely getting to know other athletes - a sort of transcendental state that I'd grown used to watching people fall into. I started chasing that state in myself.

When I say 'covering running,' I'm describing the five preceding years to 2019 following running subculture, mostly by bicycle with cameras in the basket, primarily following some of the more critically unhinged in the community - people who throw themselves into the moving traffic of a moving city, people who run hundreds of miles across humid states in the heat of summer. People whose entire lives (at least for the period of time that I had come to know them) were about how to get out over the next stretch of miles.

I have made lasting friendships in this coverage and many of these people have ended up with their accolades; first woman and second place overall in the Last Annual Vol State 500k (thank you @rhodasmoker), a trice of top ten women marathon (I see you @jmackattack, @caitlinphillips, @wicked.la), several magazine covers (hello @iamlshauntay, @samuel4nderson), inspirations that echo in the people they meet (love and more love for @matthewlukemeyer) and finally, those who had brought me to the very front of it all from the beginning (unending appreciation for @orchardstreetrunners for this).

But when I really started running, the people who showed me why I should run are people I still run with, and are the people with whom I will run to the ends of the earth - the sort of people whose skin is dusty with the slow movement of the sun across countless days, and those who chase its progress beyond the horizon under a blanket of stars until it returns the next morning. These are friends with whom I have covered countless thousands of miles. People with whom I have found religion. People who are willing to take on the steel rush of semi trucks on empty tarmac in a hundred deserts. People I can't tag, for a variety of reasons, but who all of you know.

This does not toss aside those who showed me that there is something here to chase; I would not have gotten here without them--but it does reveal the cornucopic spectra of what people find in hammering out distance. Some of us want the speed. Some of us want the distance. All of us want the free movement of the air in our lungs, and those of us who want the deserts keep finding one another out there in its emptiness, over and over.

This is what has brought me here, at least. A religion of sorts, cobbled together with shoelaces, maltodextrin, laughter, and caloric deficits. A religion I'll keep practicing because it's something holier than needing to explain it away, a religion I keep close to me because a relationship with this sort of faith in oneself doesn't require explaining to others, because those who understand already understand. If you know, you really do know.

So I'll see all of you out there sometime soon
