item.title: New York is becoming a rainy city
item.description:
New York is becoming a rainy city - a place that doesn't look like it used to, doesn't act like it used to, and won't be prepared for how it's going to be in the future - more like Seattle than what it used to be, no longer a biting temperature of winter closing and more of the form that seems to want to piss down constantly and that none of us are actually prepared to put up with.

it's funny because this is the time of year where I used to sit outside of coffeeshops for hours and hours in the mornings, somewhat reading books, somewhat reading my own mind - and this doesn't really seem possible anymore. I don't necessarily feel poorly about it, rather it's something to adapt to, something that is changing and that is going to have to lead to a new outcome.

being on vacation is it's own feeling, too - knowing full well that I don't actually need to do anything feels a little weird because it feels like admitting to myself that I don't actually need to do anything in the mean time of having decided not to do anything. I have to let myself acknowledge and let go of the feeling of thinking that I am required to come up with things that I have to do and that I need to be productive around. I don't - even if I go upstate with a guitar, a couple changes of clothes, food, books, and my notebooks and I come out of it not having done anything meaningful - that's actually fine, because that is somewhat the point of doing nothing: relaxing into a state of finding oneself in and among that which if makes us up. I'm excited by this prospect and it's something I want more of, to find peace in myself that I already have and to have that love for myself because this is something that I want out of the situation. I want to go up there and read and explore my own mind (should I bring mushrooms? maybe I should!) but the point can and will be to be with myself.

I never know who I am writing for, in fact - I used to write as though there was some audience that would read what I had to say, and I think I've moved away from that somehow, mostly out of a feeling that there is more to my own mind that deserves exploring and respecting, and I'm trying to start from this place rather than anywhere else.

Maybe at some point when you are writing for other people, you start to hear your own voice coming through whatever is sitting within it. When and if this is true, the deliberation placed into the words becomes apparent and there isn't really a reason to reject the notion of having to mean more to the words than you want to - of using the words as a form of practice rather than as a form of outward expression.

The question then becomes about crying, about feeling ripped from oneself and respecting the boundary condition that exist around the self and the expansion of the mind. Is the act of writing for others the act of telling people what you are thinking and feeling, or is it the act of arguing for a changed state of being?

If the latter, the writer has a responsibility to the reader not to tell a story, but for this story to change their mind - to present the truth as incontrovertible and then to controvert - because the Original Story is one that follows a known thread only to end up far away from it - un hilo guiando hacia otros caminos.

For the reader to come to the novel as their full selves is itself a sublime act, for a writer is required to reconcile that they arrive with the weight of their experiences and that this informa their response to what is written. As such that which is written and carried to the reader is a deeply vulnerable act of facing a stranger and telling them, earnestly

-

item.title: The Speed Project, Los Angeles → Las Vegas
item.description:
The desert gives us only a few times of year to run through it. Some of you know this for sure, as I do - I once wandered through northwestern New Mexico in late June, trying to prove I knew better, and almost gave my dog heat stroke instead. You should never argue with the sun in the summer in the desert. You'll never get a word in. The sun in the summer in the desert is too loud.

That's why running the desert in the spring is better; the Sun has not quite woken up. In March. the Sun still has a mouthful of sand and sleep-rimmed eyes. As a result, you can get in a few words before it rubs its eyes and beats down for the rest of the season like a beaming child unsullied by the anxiety of judgment.

If you want to run the desert, March in the Mojave is a good desert to test. You're more likely to survive its passage, and it will inspire you with the dreams of winter the sun has not yet shaken away. If you run the Mojave in March, you'll get to feel the weather that doesn't feel like the desert, a sideways wind that tests your core, a sleet that bounces off of a hat brim and into the shoulders of roads while you do your best to stay warm. If you run in the desert in March, at night the stars will feel as though they could swallow you whole just because they want to. You will let them, and you'll keep running over missing footsteps while chasing the flash of sky that might as well have been waiting for you to collide with it. If you run in the Mojave in March, you can look fifty miles away and run a good twenty of them and nothing will change.

If you do choose to run the Mojave in March, maybe one of those particular times you will come upon your best friend running 300 miles out of LA and you'll have to take her hand in yours to pull her 9 of those miles up a pass at the end of one of those fifty miles into a small town just outside of Vegas and the weather will lie to you the whole time as if it's the sun's favorite joke. Maybe while you walk and jog, she will fall asleep between footsteps, and you'll see faces in the mined-out cliffs you have to pass, and they will tell you stories through their layers about what the land has to offer you. You'll see those holes we make in the mountains in the chase for gold weeping out dust and chalk and you'll feel sorry for the mountains.

So you'll turn repeat the story to your friend that one of those faces in the mountain is snickering at you both for doing what you're doing. As you repeat it, the expression of that face will turn from a sneer to a grin while it reminds you both it has seen you--and any number of others--do this any number of times in the silly, long, winding story of its life. It will also remind you that you are built for grace in having chosen to take on the passage.

Maybe on this run, part of the way up the pass your friend will have to stop from all the tears that suddenly hug her old dog tight to her chest, where his memories fading are fading from her as she heals through the undertaking, while that dog in her heart put up one last defense between her and the venom an angry exit threatened to infuse in her before the escape you knew she needed. On that run, she'll live with you, the same way she lives with you, without question or sewn doubt - as though it was a calling, same as the brown of her skin choosing to commune with the dirt and to feel tired, just as tired as the dirt beneath, as though it's a form of prayer made just for this kind of motion. She will live with you in these moments as though the movement were made to remember our place in the dirt, aging downward, and your footsteps will cross Sandy Valley until you make it across the pass. Then the wind will keep screaming at you. Then the sleet will come, and the sun, and the discarded oranges that litter the side of the road.

22 miles later, when you and her and the other best friend who came to help share the ending run together toward the glass and flashing lights of the end, it might feel as though you have learned something new that wasn't there, but it may be something that lived within you since the beginning.

If running is meditation on the things that we humans leave behind (what is running, really), then running in the desert is specifically a form of communion with the things the earth has left behind. The sun leaves behind salt on the surface of a caked-out flat, and it is the same salt that gathers at the edges of our eyes. What little water reaches these places grasps onto hardy roots until they die and their skeletons litter the desert, just as our skeletons are all we leave. The wind and sun then bake it all into the to same whispered shades that lose their color, and our skin and our hair mimic this with our own passage into time.

Running in the desert is the act of choosing to bring into line aspects of the self that need changing with the time it takes to change. Relative to our lives, the changes of the desert can take an infinity - there are regions of the world where the land is only changed by the wind and the geological force of the earth moving. The desert chooses to change slowly, and running in the desert forces us to reckon with the pace at which we change. If in our short lives, we choose to sit with the change that comes over us as we move between the littered states of being, then the lessons we learn from respecting the rate of change are what running in the desert can teach us how to do. The desert is always willing to teach this lesson, but running through the desert in the spring is when you are most likely to hear it.

Having moved through that landscape will seek to place you like a seed within those layers of dirt. It will then wait patiently for a little rain and frost below a cold crust, and given the right conditions, might choose to sprout upward into the ancient explosive of crippled trees that dust the Mojave. Running in deserts feels like seeking a home in something desolate that does not care about your being there but is pleased when you are, and running through, alone, with friends, is listening for an eke of self-sufficiency in the self that seems to want to prove the possible. If you run through the desert in pursuit of yourself, it will feel like a rediscovery that over and over cracks open what you keep forgetting, and it will offer you the chance to leave behind these tawny layers with each forward footfall.

If you run through the Mojave in March, you might then share that end with so many others who sought the same end, and you might all have might have learned similar lessons. You'll laugh and share them, and these will be the friends you make in the desert. These will be the people who listened to the same whisper of sand they tried to keep out of their toes, and you'll commiserate over the experience of arguing with a sleepy sun and the weather that follows it. You'll laugh and share, and filled with the sunlight of early spring will make plans to do it again just so that you can see everyone do it again, and you'll all smile through the wrinkles the sun is offers as parting gifts - because yes, it really was better next year, and it was even better the year after.

item.title: Out at the edge of the L5 cluster
item.description:
Out at the edge of the L5 cluster, someone turned on an orbital zero-friction ion drive in just the right place and the Path was seen for the first time - a bright green flash that was hanging in orbit, then dimmed to a six-hundred-kilometer streak leading away from Earth. Science craft parked themselves around green light for a number of months, aiming to gather measurements of whatever it was that had been sparked into being around ignition, but any sensor type was only capable of detecting a 555 nanometer wavelength hanging in the air with no source - simply emerald green light floating in fixed orbit, without a source.
What made the beam more interesting than an immaculately conceived lightbeam sitting in space was that it changed direction with the orbit of earth around the planet, fixed on an unknown location off in the distance, wavering with the change of the L5's place in orbit.

The positioning of the beam relative to the earth's own orbit presented a problem. When the sun and the earth occluded the path, it showed up as a harmless 4-kilometer-wide beam that passed directly though anything in its path, inexplicably illuminating the insides of buildings as it passed through - but anything in the path would be cast in a fixed level of brightness that engulfed everything. Those who lived in its occlusion path would complain that they couldn't escape the light, but there was no getting around it - when the beam passed through the Earth, everything was green.
This lead to a divergence in responses - most populations sitting in the path of occlusion migrated away from this annoyance once the novelty had worn off - others thought that the beam was a sign from their god and that because of this, they should live directly in the path of the light. The science said nothing - it was harmless green light, but an annoyance, and there was nothing do be done about it, and no escaping the light if you were in its path - but green-light research centers as well built themselves into the occlusion path in order to better understand properties of the light.
About two years after the beam flashed into being, observers still paying attention noticed as well that the beam was slowly moving along its fixed trajectory, leading sages in Elysium City to plot the beam's trajectory out of our system, and to it's eventual name as 'The Path'. The movement of the beam was measurably slow - on the order of at less than a meter per year, but work put into measurement proved that this movement was accelerating over time - prompting sages to call for bigger investment from their parishes to study the phenomenon in the hopes that it would be understood before it accelerated out of our system. A number of probes were sent out ahead of its path as well - many-paneled stations built to either prepare for its passing, or in the assumed trajectory of its movement.

After ten years, the Path's movement had accelerated to a rate of two hundred meters per year with no sign of deceleration, and no progress had been made on the meaning of either the trajectory or of the beam itself - the rate of acceleration was too high for any meaningful propulsion mechanism to catch up once it was to reach high speed, and there was no telling if it would accelerate to the some unknown physical constant.

-

item.title: The Hidden Continent (excerpt)
item.description:
"Listen, I'm not really sure if this woman is on drugs or something, but we tested her and there's nothing in her system to indicate that she is."
"Ok - so what, you want me to talk to her? Why?"
"It's what she's talking about - she's acting like it's really urgent."
"George, it's LA. We have a lot of strung out people who believe a lot of this shit."
"That's what I thought too - but then she did something. I think you need to see it. It's not what you think. I didn't believe it either, but she did it a number of times and I'm not sure what to think. You have to talk to her."
"George, please be sure this isn't a waste of our time."
"Look, I would call a lot of the things that we've had to deal with in the last six months a waste of time, but I have a gut feeling about this. I don't think this is going to be a waste of time. Just talk to her. Just for a second. "

They unlocked the door to the interrogation room and there, sitting in the provided chair, was a slight woman, eyes a little bit cagey, but striking. Dark black hair, a strong, curved nose, dark skin in the way of leather heavy, driven eyes staring right through his own. Something about them - not quite a fire - more a question of knowing, something powerful that seemed to bely a knowledge. Wizened, but tired. He extended his hand.

"Well alright, hello, my name is Detective Harrow. I'm with the Federal Bureau of Investigations. I'm not sure how you were able to convince the people who called me, but I hear that you're here to talk about magic? What was your name?"
She looked back at him, her eyes sparking.
"My name is Leta."
"Ok, nice to meet you Leta. I apologize for all the formality to do with making you wait. However, you're quite persistent and you've been really patient, so I'm glad to make the time here. How can we help you?"
"My people are dying. No one knows, this needs to change."
He looked at her, pausing.
"Ma'am, have you had a drug test?"
She didn't react.
"Have you taken any medication today?"
A moment passed before she looked up at him, opening a mouth that didn't belong in cities and looked instead like someone who had spent years in the sun.
"My people are dying. I did not want to come here. I did not want to do this. I did not want to speak with you and show you what has happened but we cannot fix this on our own and we must fix it."

item.title: The Two Types of Internet
item.description:
a bit of a ramble on the direction I think the internet might be headed. I think we'll see two things. 1. Consumer internet most people will spend their time here, but generally speaking it will lack in much social depth. I think in part this will be the realm of the creator economy and adspace, where the goal is to make things that people want, or to find things that you want. It will mostly be a domain of parasocial interaction or direct consumerism, and will orient itself mostly around good user experiences and not much user input. It is generally not interoperable because it is a domain where platforms compete for market share, and the best way to do so will be to silo interactions into walled gardens. Users will generally not contribute their thoughts and opinions here, and the computer literacy will stay low in general. General examples: Instagram, TikTok, Pinterest, YouTube, Snapchat, etc. 2. Community internet These will be smaller corners of the internet where people who are literate in how to use all different manner of communication will create community across any number of platforms; the social layer will act (acts) as an interoperability mechanism since those who are in this space take their time to build relationships with one another, agnostic of medium. The barrier to access will be some degree of internet-native computer literacy, both socially and practically. Tech that is used here is a means to an end, and those involved will always be communities of intention. It's from these communities that new social coordination mechanisms will form that can operate on a digitally local level that does not care about the limitations of meatspace. More "interesting" things will be made here that generally will work to bring people closer to ideals Examples of this kind of internet are most of crypto and true FOSS, some science communities, Farcaster, Mastodon, and many subject area Discords and Subreddits, and will work best when they do not aim for popularity but rather functionality, since too large of anything becomes operatively diluted in utility. -- Both of these are ultimately good things, and characteristic of humans slowly evolving back toward tribal tendencies while using technologies that we made but did not have the social tools to adapt to. A consumer internet could result in people spending less time online, since they realize that they are not truly interacting with others and will spend more time interacting in meatspace, but it's equally likely people will doomscroll these environments. My hope is that socially we'll evolve past this, but that's just optimism. The countervailing force could be a heterogenous Community Internet, where select people who want to find their people can move with intention toward those who hold similar ideals, and will make meaningful things together. These communities will be small-bit-mighty, and will likely have enormous areas of effect on a Consumer Internet, since it will be a place for people to organize. I could also foresee competition between these internets, mostly due to a Consumer Internet wanting eyeballs and despising the organizational effects of there being spaces to organize online (this, I think, is actually what the purchase of X was about). -- Time will tell, but I think the greatest differentiating factor between the types of people that will occupy these internets will be based on the many forms on literacy, sociality, and collaborative tendencies. People will occupy both spaces in many cases, one out of obligation to a society that has integrated internet-as-media and the other out of a desire to find our tribes - but I hope that this works broadly in our favor. Generally, I think it will.

Crucial to this working is developing a sense of what online culture can look like in its many facets and how people can learn to navigate online spaces as either newcomers or as collaborators. Some communities will operate privately and only by invitation, while others will be inviting and places where others are attracted to feeling included - but I think all of this will evolve out of a human desire to create communities around mutually assured survival. I think there is a high potential that a good Community Internet might work toward better coordination despite individual differences in belief, in stark contrast to the feed-based internet that we had in the Social Media era that amplified discontent bringing us back to a time when humans simply dissociated from one another in situations of discontent. It will be difficult to determine whether or not it's working - tribes can still go to war with one another, after all - but maybe we'll have just a few less reasons to oppose those we're in community with than we do when faced with a feed of literally every other person on the planet.

item.title: On Seeking Utopias
item.description:
There's something to be said for the pull away from cynicism we’re beginning to see from the enabling effects of the new internet.

In some sense, the dystopian leanings of our predictions for humanity are starting to feel too prescient - we are living within these predictions rather than seeing them as some far-flung reality, and the experience is exhausting. It is a grueling existence made somehow more disheartening by the fact that the irrationality of humans rears its head again and again in face of what most would consider to be rational action.

So what can we do with the knowledge that we knew we would be living in the reality we are now experiencing, and that yes, indeed, it is our fault, and that yes, we also know what causes our course toward dystopia in the first place? All this in mind - extrapolations of our present into future, all the more far-flung and depressing as dystopian, must offer us pause. Do we want things to continue on course toward the fictional realities that we didn't expect to materialize? Do we let them? How much of it is under our control?

The last question I find the most urgent - if we know that present conditions are likely to keep us careening in the direction of disaster, and that we are here at our own hand - how much control are we willing to give up in the course toward a collective future, and what hand does any individual person have in ownership over control of this future?

Much of dystopian writing has us completely lacking in control - often because the faults that create a cause for dystopias have already happened, or the protagonists have little to no control over when or if they do. Any dystopia is written from an absence of control. Control is the protagonist in overcoming the conditions of being lacking thereof - admission to higher, more insidious or chaotically evil forces determine the setting. Hypercapitalist dystopias lead us into futures that elide control from individuals into a total obedience of market pressures and consumption, encouraging people to mean nothing but vectors for financial lifeblood. This is the extension of the present - capitalism alone in control, with individuals under its servitude - a financial market for every engagement and action in the material (and digital) world.

Disaster dystopias are not so different - where the bomb has already fallen, the plague has already destroyed society, the supervolcano has blotted out the sun. Here, hope can only take form in society, navigating the ashes, carving out control against the uncontrollable reality of disaster - and the solutions, paradises, or arcs for a story of exit all exist within the bounds of what is possible with disaster in control of the present. To find optimism against the face of disaster is to inspire hope in action - top take control of what little over which we can exert pressure. Optimism is a weapon against these stark realities, it is the only weapon through which to fight great improbabilities - the Hakagure's samurai facing off against certain death with no regard for their own life.

At the root of these inspired realities is a common theme - that we are not in control of the futures toward which we guided. Either we are led there by a blind and collective fault to which no individual holds blame, or there is a great external pressure over which our fates are stretched.

The most hopeful and the least human of these stories are seen as youthful fantasy - it's a hallmark of young adult fiction for a party of individuals or an individual to have sufficient control over the future that they might avoid, prove, or solve great calamity and thus save the world. That's why it's entertaining in the first place - it seems so improbable that any one group of people could both act enough in the best interest of humanity and have enough control to change the fate of the realities that we experience. It feels naïve, and it is. No one person could truly hold sufficient power to change the future, because no one person could ever hold so much control.

I think the greatest fear of humanity is to be in control and fail. It's a recurring theme in all aspects of improvement on societal and individual levels - that the hardest part of existing is giving up a desire for control when we don't have it. We hinge all aspiration on the illusion of control, and we learn to overcome frustration when we realize that we do not have control.

An Eightfold Path walks toward absolution along a tightrope of personal discipline (control) and willingness to allow existence to proceed without your influence (control). The opiate quality of a higher power, too, is thematic because the greatest situational grace for an individual is to relinquish control of their life to the determinism of a deity - to seek out calm in the recognition of a deterministic designer who can guide the present toward their intended future. Again - control of fate being handed off from the individual (or indeed the collective, with respect to the congregation) to something outside of the individual - because this makes a future that we could be in control of that much more palatable when it isn't in our favor, and puts us less at fault.

Optimism seems to sprout and grow when we take ownership over our direction - when an individual future is something toward which one person can steer, because the rudder is in their hand. There is hope in being called to action - there optimism in appreciating control as an enabling force. When we believe that we can guide fate, much more is possible. Problems feel smaller, more attainable, futures much more a vehicle for our hopes to arrive in, utopias all the more achievable.

When, then, does optimism have to do with sovereignty over control, and how does this apply to collectives, not individuals? Even blind optimism is giving oneself control over willingness to see things proceed in the most favorable direction, though not by our hand, instead by fate. But I am arguing for a more urgent sense of optimism, one that places control back in the hands of collectives, so that individuals feel that they can indeed have influence and guide collectives toward utopias.

The reason utopias feel naïve is due to an inspired sense that we are not in control - that we don't hold the keys to the future. What, then, if we allowed ourselves to believe that we did?

Dystopias do not exist when collectives are in control of the story and the futures being acted upon are in the interest of collectives. Agency is the greatest power we hold as individuals - the liberty to move freely and make choices. Dystopias sprout and fester around a lack of agency - we as individuals cannot move the path. The arc of success against dystopia is the defeat of the forces that impose dystopia and therefore maintain control. Liberty is gaining, once again, the control that you rightly deserve as an individual. Collective utopias are born from collaboration in the hands of independent agents. Cynicism against being a utopian is born from a cynicism over whether or not you have control.

How do we conceive of utopias as something attainable, when so many are under the impression that we do not have control? If it's emblematic of the present era that the futures in which we are trained are outside of our control, what better way to cope with this reality than to view hope with cynicism, and continue to believe that we indeed do not have control?

This is why systems that enable the greatest individual sovereignty precourse utopias. As it stands, we no longer feel in control of the future, and instead hope that some displaced outside hero will resolve over our present to lead us from dystopia in a hero’s journey. The truth is far more urgent, and far more in the hands of those who read this.

The power of one's own agency roots itself in immovable earth against a lack of control - the willingness to remain immobile against the flows that surround us is a protest against cynicism and giving up hope. If this is true, the agency of hopeful collectives enable even greater control over collective fate. We can then measure attainment of the much grander, more expansive utopias that agency-based optimism offers us.

We deserve utopias, but we specifically deserve several. We deserve a hopeful version of the future that is under our control, where we harness collective agency to achieve what seems under our present cynicism to be impossible. It is only impossible if we believe that reaching utopias is outside of our control.

The greatest problems of our age are borne out of giving up control to others, and some of our greatest achievements have been in favor of this control being defeated and sovereignty - liberty - returned to individuals and collectives. Climate change is a coordination problem, but it is also a problem of control - we do not believe that it is something on which we can exert control. We believe that there are other forces at play that determine the outcome. If this is true - indeed we are dystopia bound, but I do not believe that the human capacity for agency can be so easily defeated. Instead, it must be nurtured.

An agency for collectives to build away from dystopias and toward utopias requires that they, too, have agency, both in the futures that they experience and the missions that they take on with others. Technologies that enable agency are therefore imperative - because the tools of agency are what inspire an individual with the truth that they do indeed have control. Tools that we do not need to trust to control us, even more so - because tools in whose operation we have no doubt of subterfuge over our agency cannot take control from us.

We do not possess many tools that do not manipulate us in turn - we have not made many of them with intention. In the progress of human society, we must see carefully what great agency can be offered to individuals by our tools as well as the potential in these tools for robbing control that may lie in wait from their use. Oftentimes we can't predict these faults, but ownership over our mistakes is equally pressing - if we are inspired (as collectives and as individuals) to believe that we have a hand in the mistakes of humanity, we can atone for them, even learn and grow from them. To believe that there is no ownership over collective fault is dire at best, so it is imperative that we are inspired with a culture of ownership that documents and hardens ownership over our faults. If we maintain that we do not have a hand in our own mistakes, we can never seek to improve from them, and then all arguments to do so seem baseless.

It may be that the greatest human achievement is to seek means through which individuals feel collective utopias are attainable - and that these utopias are born from human intention, from the hands of individuals and collectives, and in the interest of all those that utopias must serve. Great hope unfolds from the believe that potential is an achievement at the hand of collectives, and utopias can only be achieved if great hope is afforded as a function of working toward utopias; people must be enabled to believe that utopias are possible because they themselves are capable of creating them.

item.title: Orbweaver
item.description:
It was about ten feet long, mottled grey, and had the same texture as granite. I think if I hadn't known about stone already, I'd have uncovered it and wouldn't have known that it didn't belong there, but a 4-year degree in geology leading to a masters in schist incursions told me otherwise. Besides, it didn't really feel like granite. There was something about it that felt at once less dense, but far heavier - as though it had the weight of an object, not a part of the landscape.

There was also something about it that told me I shouldn't tell anyone I'd found it. On the surface of it, sure, it was probably a little weird that a geology professor from a local college was spending their weekends digging pilot cores in the a neighborhood state park - but something told me that it was more than this. It wasn't until I uncovered it that it really clicked - I'd spent a week carefully peeling back the layers to reveal whatever had broken the tip of my spiral bore - but this realization had me settled in knowing that whatever this was was more than just a curiosity.

When I first figured out its total size, I didn't know what to do. I didn't have the skills to understand what to do next, so I took a ridiculous number of photographs. Somehow I was motivated to take these on film rather than digitally, as though taking pains to make sure that there wasn't a trace that I'd found this thing in the woods. This was echoed by how I covered the object back up, building a lattice of branches and covering it in dead leaves. I wasn't too worried someone would stumble on what I'd found, it was in a strange spot and at best, maybe a dog would run over to the area and piss on it.

When I developed the photos in my darkroom, things started to feel a bit more ominous. The images showed something completely different from what I'd photographed. In place of quiet-looking stone, there was a sleek, ornate, organic shape that approximated a minimal surface egg, a mathematical object that I'd remembered from the Topology courses I took alongside my master's program. It was a gunmetal gray, swiss-cheesed with paths through the object, and there was no way that this had developed naturally - the filigree-like pathways through the object made it appear symmetrical, all the more organic. There was no way this was a rock.

Also, the photographs had the object standing up.

When the first photos developed, this was the part that struck me with the most dissonance. The photographs looked as though I'd taken them of the object while it was standing on this end, several steps back in order to capture the entirety of the shape in frame. Worse yet, I couldn't shake the feeling that it was looking at me through the image - the same feeling a person has when they look back on a portrait of a friend looking directly into the frame - but I couldn't discern where the eyes might be. The whole thing seemed as though it was staring into the lens.

It was about 8pm when I developed the first images - just the time that the state park closed. After I'd gotten over the chill feeling of not knowing that sat in the forefront of my chest, so similar to a feeling of devastation, I packed a flashlight, a strobe, and my jacket, hopping back into my car to drive back toward the object. I ended up having to park in the middle school parking lot, toward the back, hoping that the car seemed inconspicuous, knowing that it probably wasn't - but when I drove into the lot there were no police patrolling the area, so I tried my luck. I was lucky that my training had me noting down the lat/long coordinates of my pet neighborhood incursion studies, having logged the location of the dig into a fitness watch, but I hadn't taken this approach to the site, and it was dark, and it was late November. There would be some bushwhacking involved.

I walked about a hundred feet into the woods guided by the watch, careful to let my eyes adjust, before I flipped on my flashlight in bug-proof mode and bathed the forest in front of me in red light. It clicked for me that I was doing something unusual - but the power that intrigue had over me was substantial. I was compelled, methodically stepping over the macabre shadows of logs and pushing aside bushes and branches, following the dim arrow on the LED surface of my watch with its proximity decreasing.

I watched the distance tick to zero, my mind finally growing accustomed to a recognition of my surroundings in a different light, and sure enough - the lattice of sticks and leaves were still over laying across my dig site. I reached into the loam I'd piled up in a corner of the site to pull out a rake I'd brought with me several digs before and began to clear away the cover I'd built. The object definitely wasn't standing. I took the photographs out of the backpack I'd brought with me, flipping the flashlight to natural glow, and again, the image of the object standing erect in the woods, light passing through the gaps, stared back at me from the photograph.

I decided to risk taking more photographs. I realized before I thought about doing so that I'd fully uncovered the object again, and before pulling out my camera, I shone my flashlight over the surface of the object. It looked no different than it had before, a granite-like texture that I couldn't place.

I set up my strobe - stepping back from the pit I'd dug up and positioned myself to take the image. Nothing was different. I looked around the woods, hoping nothing was looking back at me, but curiosity and a little bit of fear goaded me onward. It was not probable anyone would see the strobe go off unless they were in the woods with me. That was a chance I'd have to take.

I armed the strobe and the remote transmitter, stepped back, setting my focus at the distance I knew I was from the object, and depressed the shutter. One technique that I'd learned from shooting was to keep both eyes open when aiming, so that an object's framing in the final image matches what you see. The strobes went off.

For a split second, I knew I saw something other than what I'd been aiming at. The strobed image on my retina was of the object, on its end, lit against the night sky, long, tendrilled shadows passing through the objects holes. It wasn't what I'd come into the woods to find. Fuck. There was no way that just happened.

I stepped over to the dig pit, and the object clearly hadn't moved. Fear started creeping into my chest, but I stepped back to take another photograph. It didn't make any sense. I was aiming downward, but the image on my retina was looking upward, at the object against the canopy; not the image I was about to take again.

I held my breath, finger slowly pushing down the shutter. The strobe fired, and again, stark against my retinas was the object, staring back at me from a frame of the canopy against stars. There's no way this is happening.

I didn't know what to do. I lowered the camera and looked at the object, still lying in situ. It hadn't moved, there was no way that it had moved. I hesitated, breath tight in my chest. Looked down at my watch.

It was 3am. I'd been in the woods for 9 hours. There's no way this is happening.

I packed up my things. Something told me to cover the object back up, but I was terrified. Something was happening, here, something I didn't have words for, and that I knew no one would understand if I explained to them - it could only be if I showed them. When the object was covered back up, I stood back, looking at my dig site again. Fuck. I turned and began walking back, and immediately realized I hadn't logged the location of the parking lot or my track through the woods. FUCK.

Calm down. I pulled out my phone, pulled open my maps application. I wasn't far, I just had to head in the general direction of the lot. Thank goodness for technology. Fuck.

40 minutes slogged by. I didn't recognize anything I'd walked over getting to the site. Nothing looks the same in reverse. I kept checking my phone, every twenty feet or so, inching closer to the lot. Fuck. Terror was building in me. What the fuck did I just find?

At the edge of the lot, I saw my car, cloistered toward the edge of the lot. No police in the lot. Good. I walked toward my car, opened up the trunk, put down my things, opened the driver's side door, sat down. What the fuck did I just find? Turned on the car engine. What the fuck did I just find?

item.title: I watched a boat fly past
item.description:
I watched a boat fly past on glassy lake surface, towing behind a single-blade water skier. The boat was a fishing boat rather than the kind that I usually see up here in the summer, that bright metal hull cutting through the lake and leaving behind the only set of waves I'd seen that morning so far, a thin line plying out from the bow as it crossed my line of sight.

The wake slowly expanded as the boat cozied off to the left with the skier in tow. With the humidity in the air, the mountains in the background looked like an extension of the lake, the wake a single line torn through and widening toward and against me, up toward the horizon.

I have loved the waves finally hitting the shoreline and their pattern suddenly repeating against themselves, the parallel lines repeating inward into a lace of diamond patterns; how do the waves remember once they've hit the shore? Even against the break of stones and sand, how do waves remember fractions of what they once were?

It's this principle of opposite and equal reaction that continues to puzzle me, even after the dissipating action of coming into contact with your environment, the pieces of who you are continue to reverberate within the body of water that we call the soul. Those diamonds of calm, crises rising into overlapping peaks, maybe the patterns of the self that form come up from whatever comes from connecting those ripples - the unique nature of self-becoming as a composition of where the peaks intersect. Interlinked.

Why at the end of a day is there enough wind to whip up the waves, starting from glass, but then reaching for calm again as the sun sets - I've never understood this, why at the end of a day somehow the lake also seems to calm down and see a need for others to feel this same calmness. It's some sort of blessing.

item.title: Containment
item.description:
I got three steps into the first chamber before I realized that I'd made a mistake, and that the door closing behind me was something I wasn't comfortable with. From the crinkling sound of the suit, the temperature in the room was lower than I had realized it was, and the plastic immediately stiffened. I knew it was only a matter of time and lack of movement that the temperature would get lower and lower. I wasn't wearing enough clothes and the negative pressure fan was not going to help, pulling in cold, filtered air.

"You ok, Ahrens?"

"Yeah. Yes," I lied. No way out of here but forward.

I walked toward a bright white laminate desk, littered with papers, notebooks, and a microscope. A single dim orange lamp cast a warm glow into the shadows of the surrounding room. In the center of the desk was a small metal container with a ring of dust around it that looked as though it had exploded out of the container, creating a dark gray halo around where it lay, gray fingerprints tracing around the edges of the dust. He was sitting there, grey skinned, immobile, hands on the arms of the his chair, staring into nothing, until his eyes looked up at me again. Red ringed the outside of his irises.

"Hell of a day for this to happen."

His voice sounded like paint dust, his lips barely moving. I kept my distance, hesitant.

"You know, I really didn't think you'd end up being the one coming in here. I'm sorry that it's you."

I nodded inside the negative pressure suit, which he didn't see.

"Yeah. ... yeah."

"Look I don't like this any more than you do, and there ain't nothin we can do right now but try to figure it out. Obviously I don't think I have a ton of time left to think about it with you"

"Right"

"We don't know who sent us this, obviously, but we you and I both know what it is. We have to hope like hell that it didn't make its way out of the room."

"Yeah"

"So I want to know, are they planning for it. Are they worried about it. Did they listen to my instructions"

I relaxed a little bit.

"Yeah. There's an electromagnetic containment device over the whole building. The CDC scrambled a little bit getting a containment bubble that was big enough, but you've only been here for like twelve hours, so ... I guess that's pretty fast."

"Right. We have to hope like hell that was fast enough. You and I both know it probably wasn't."

I nodded. He was probably right. This stupid suit was probably not enough to make it safe, either. I knew that. We well knew that. Again, he didn't see my nod due to the plastic visor.

"Yeah. I'm... yeah. Dr Budoise, I'm so sorry. I really am."

"Ain't nothin. This was probably going to happen, right."

Silence rang out for a second, he looked at me again.

"But we have to do everything we can to prevent it from getting worse. Back in the 50's, even when they were afraid the bombs would drop any day, the saying was always 'You should still go out and plant a tree'. You have to hold on to hope, Ahrens."

"And we don't have much time. You and I both know that. I think I've got about ten minutes in me."

The only parts of him that were moving were his mouth and his eyes, and he'd been speaking with as much care to move as little as possible, but I could see the cracks forming along his jawline.

"What's interesting though, is that I can't really feel anything happening. My wondering is if they're eating away at the least important processes first, turning them into raw materials, and leaving as much possible functional for as long as possible. Like, I'd have thought I'd want to cough, but so far, seems like my lungs are pretty clear. They seem to want to keep that going. Vocal cords though, I ain't too sure."

I didn't really know what to do. We were doing everything we could. There was a probability that in the time it took to seal off the building, some of the dust had floated out of the room. I'd been downstairs in the wet lab, sealed off. I hadn't taken off my negative pressure suit in almost a day.

"But I'll be all right, ain't nothin doing. I hope you'll be all right"

"Yeah."

item.title: Slept near the VLA last night
item.description:
"Slept near the VLA last night. That must be why this place feels so otherworldly. Our dogs are having the best time, the backdrop of a stellar observatory, and the easy crackling of a morning fire.
There are not many better things than this, and things that are, I've not yet experienced. Self-reliance gives us a sense of balance, and of unity where all else seems to fail providence. The emotion of this landscape and of these mornings, such as they are, this is the true essence of love. This is the freedom granted by finding oneself detached from the rest of humanity, where the world of the individual meets the whole damned universe.
This is the place where one can feel important, where conclusions can be drawn with a proper understanding of their scale and implication. There's not much to it, only separating oneself adequately to find that sense of self-importance, but as well to recognize one's connection to the grand machine that surrounds us."
(written at the Very Large Array, 2015)--

item.title: Metafiction
item.description:
Metafiction is a form of writing wherein the writer often breaks the fourth wall by playing with the structure of narrative to pull the reader into the act of reading. It’s something that is often seen in the writing of Kundera, M, but as well in Cortazar, J and Labatut, B.

With Kundera, M in particular, the metafictional elements are present in his divergences into philosophical footnotes and/or commentary on the story itself, particular with the effort to have the reader understand that the motivation of the story is to have the reader consume the universe that has been created around characters or narrative, but instead as a vehicle for thoughts and ideas that the writer holds.

*ed: it’s also a form of writing that I particularly enjoy and would like to get better at, because it’s a writing style that I think I’d really enjoy to write in. In particular, I could see The Cruft existing as a piece of metafictional work that uses the musings of a hyperintelligence (currently named Hayelek) who exists in a state of observing or remarking on the phenomenon of a failed civilization that once might have existed on Earth - however the general sense that I get is that Hayelek will be more the observer while The Figure will be the one making philosophical asides - which brings our total characters in the book up to three rather than two.

item.title: Time vs Money
item.description:
In order to get things done, there are basically two pressures: Time and Money

When you do not have time, you have to spend it preciously. When you have too much time, you will waste it.

  • this notion comes from understanding that broadly, it's hard to urge forward a system if it's trying to grow under conditions that threaten its ability to exist. This will result in quick movement in vectors that preserve the system to the best of the ability for it to stabilize and maintain itself.

  • If, by contrast, time is abundant, then there will be little effort by the system to do more than expand readily, taking chances in directions that might not actually favor the system at large, resulting in a need for the system to respond by reorienting toward the highest-value paths in times of scarcity.

When you need to make money, you will work harder toward earning it. When you have money, you will work harder spending it.

  • When resources are scarce but a system is still in need of them, the system will work to do two things: gain its resources as widely as possible, and use the resources at its disposal to move in the direction of the largest possible source of those resources.
  • If, on the other hand, resources are plentiful, it's less likely that the system will have to work hard to allocate resources effectively toward the corporeal needs that are the highest priority. This results in the same issue that we see with the abundance of time - the system grows too widely and the misuse of resources results in outcomes that spread resources thin in an attempt to spread across a possible domain as widely as possible.

With these in mind, it's important to note that in times of abundance, chances are taken that may be costly when scarcity approaches. these two forces will happen in concert and will result in opposing degrees of preparedness on the part of the system - knowing full well that the approach is always unlikely to be perfect and that some degree of failure needs to be tolerated in order for chances to keep the system surviving.

The notion that systems should move perfectly is inorganic - it is not in line with the ways that natural systems function. Recombination in times of abundance means that the cause for more variation can result in resilience, but the meaning of this resilience is only apparent in times of scarcity.

This means that when approaching the notion of how to build out a system effectively, it's increasingly important to take chances when there is a lot at your disposal, but it's equally important to be ready to eat the sacrifices that emerge as a result of this when scarcity comes around. It cannot seem like a failure, but rather a lesson, and a meaningful one at that.

This is why in times of crisis, the most important tracks are the ones that have been used and re-used. Access and examine the paths that have been used before and refine them. Scarcity is a cruel, but diligent teacher. Be sure to be one that is listening when it offers a lesson, and dig into what you know in order to push forward.

item.title: a classroom argument about learning
item.description:
She piped up from the back of the room, standing up.

"Well - professor, if you'll let me say it - I think all of us agree that none of us knew we'd end up here. I don't think it's fair for us to talk about our current conditions as though there was something we could have done to prevent it. None of us knew that what we were doing would have these results."

I cocked a slight smile, keeping my eyes locked in her direction.

"Continue?"

"So like - We act as though we should all feel bad for how things turned out, but I'm just not really convinced that it was something we could have done anything about. Everything was proceeding to this point, and now we're here. There's not a lot we can do to walk back the idea of changing where we are. It feels like the best thing we can do is start from where we are."

Another voice spoke up, a boy sitting in the third row. Rimmed glasses.

"It's not really about us atoning for what we did, I don't think that's what the professor is trying to have us understand. We need to know how we got to where we are so that we can work to dismantle the structures that are resulting in the present. We can't really change things right now unless we know how we got here."

She hesitated, looked back at me.

"Do you want to respond to that?"

"Yeah - like, I get the idea there, and I'm not disagreeing with it at all. I think we definitely need to know what brought us here, but look at what we learned this semester. A lot of things are random, some of the reasons that things are happening have more to do with the interaction of two or three events that had unpredictable outcomes. I'm not just convinced that we can find the answer in looking at the past."

There was some silence.

"Why might that be?"

"I - well, I think that there's value in it, but the random nature of our time puts us in the condition of trying to explain a present that is currently unfolding. My impression is that by trying to decipher too much of what it took for right now to happen might result in a constant state of reflection rather than one of action. I think if we're instead looking at the present and deciding what needs to happen next, then maybe we can get ahead of things getting any worse."

The boy in the rimmed glasses responded again.

"We can't look at the present without understanding how the present came to be the present,"

"And I'm not arguing with that, I know there's a degree of that, I just - I don't think that it's what we should be obsessed with. There's too much at stake for us to want to get through and too many dangers of us continuing on with the way things are right now."

"An obsession with how the past unfolded is what all science is based on, though. You can't solve the present without having done analysis of the past. The idea that you can work from the present without having to know that seems short-sighted."

She faltered a bit. The boy with the rimmed glasses sat back down, looking back at me.

"Our current condition is a result of the actions we took in our past. This is true. I think Mr Sales is correct to bring up that some degree of analysis is incontrovertibly important to the process of examining any path forward from a disposition. Looking into the past and tabulating the work that took us toward certain ill-conceived outcomes is crucial,"

"However, while I think you're both right in your own ways, but what Ms Reedin just said is more correct than you are, Mr Sales. What she is right to point out is in opposition to your core position. We cannot recreate the past, therefore we cannot hope to create the future from a knowledge of the past."

I could see Sales squirm in his seat, hoping to respond.

"This does not mean that we don't need to know the past, it means that we are obliged to understand that correcting course on the issues that are ahead of us requires new ways of thinking that are more resourceful than the ones we have employed so far,"

"Resourcefulness requires courage, and courage is illogical. It's possible to make measured guesses at what you think will happen in most situations, but some degree of faith is necessary in order to get toward the solutions we hope to see unfold. There is no certainty. That is what I've hoped to teach you all in this course, which is why Ms Reedin's comment on present disposition is where I want us to start from. What are the basics? What are we starting from, and what tools do we have at our disposal?"

Sales blurted out

"But our tools are the past!"

"This is true, some of the past can be used as a tool. However, you are committing the sin of overfitting - you are believing that past trends can somehow predict future outcomes. Any scientist worth their salt will tell you this is not true, and that the results themselves as they unfold are more truthful than a study of the past. Ms Reedin's comment has us understand that we need to consider the variety of optionality that the present offers us, because there is potential in understanding that a path forward from the present can be informed by any approach, meaning that it's possible for us to completely change our approach in opposition to any and all past proceeding. It's very likely that a resolution to our current condition lies in taking the problem from a completely different angle, approaching it with some other tool than prediction. Sometimes, if you want to knock something off course, you need to blow something else up, and this, more than anything else, lies in doing the unexpected."

item.title: elliptical writing
item.description:
Per Kundera, M, elliptical writing is the act of not-writing everything that you intend to have as a part of your text, the you should indeed leave some of the imagining up to interpretation on the part of the reader.

It's for this reason that slice-of-life style writing is a useful vehicle for introducing people to stories - rather than completely covering an idea end-to-end, there's a way for the writing to encompass only that which is directly relevant so that there's a way for the reader to expand what exists beyond what they have written on their own.

In fact, this is one of the more powerful notions when it comes to writing, to give your reader something that they can interpret and build out, and further is the very reason that it's valuable to flesh everything out as a writer, but then only write about what is important.

Elliptical writing has us drop into a story and fill in the rest of the characters and setting with our own imagination, a way of building something beautiful out of the idea of beauty itself, rather than the literal imposition of beauty upon the observer.
